1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, the tenth day of the month, that certain of the elders of Israel came to enquire of the Lord, and sat before me. Then came the word of the Lord unto me, saying, Son of man, speak unto the elders of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Are ye come to enquire of me? As I live, saith the Lord God, I will not be enquired of by you. Wilt thou judge them, son of man, wilt thou judge them? cause them to know the abominations of their fathers: And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; In the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up mine hand unto the seed of the house of Jacob, and made myself known unto them in the land of Egypt, when I lifted up mine hand unto them, saying, I am the Lord your God; In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands: Then said I unto them, Cast ye away every man the abominations of his eyes, and defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt: I am the Lord your God. But they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me: they did not every man cast away the abominations of their eyes, neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt: then I said, I will pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt. But I wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, among whom they were, in whose sight I made myself known unto them, in bringing them forth out of the land of Egypt.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the chapter's plan as a historical survey of rebellion in Egypt and the desert through both generations, with forbearance only for the divine name's sake; Ellicott observes that the elders never actually put their question and that the answer meets an unspoken concern for the nation, quotes Jerome on the difference between those who ask rightly and men like these, makes the doubled question an imperative and judging mean preferring charges, admits that neither the command against idolatry in Egypt nor the rebellion against it survives in the law while arguing both are implied by the covenant and by the order to go out and sacrifice, and concedes how strange the title of glory looks after centuries of misrule.

Gill counts the interval to the day from the prophet's call and his last oracle, and puts the sparing as honour rather than merit; Calvin insists this is plain history and not vision, contrasts the one channel appointed for this people with the soothsayers and augurs the nations used, rejects as strained the construction that takes one verb in two senses, holds that such men are to be dismissed rather than argued with since the Spirit does not always strive, notes that the exhortation to hope had been given and a witness of the deliverance stood among them, and states hardest of all that the sparing came of regard for a name that would else be a laughing-stock.

Clarke gives the chapter's outline, adds that the last five verses belong with the next chapter, renders the refusal as declining to hear or have anything to do with them, explains the lifted hand as the gesture of an oath surviving in his own country's courts, notes that the lawgiver did not mention the Egyptian idolatry, and pictures a father surveying countries to find his children a home; Wesley notes how little time was left before the siege, suspects the delegation had settled beforehand what it meant to do, prefers an arm made bare for deliverance, and calls the phrase about milk and honey proverbial.

Henry contrasts this occasion with an earlier discourse, that one answering presumptuous reflections and this hypocritical enquiries, thinks the exact dating deliberate so that captives might keep count and see the years creeping toward release, and finds the shape of the whole Bible in the sequence, a creature's rebellion following at once on his making, calling this nation a representation of mankind in its dealings with God and his with it.

debates.question: Why does the law contain no record of the Egyptian idolatry charged here?

positions.position: Both the command and the rebellion are implied, by the covenant the mission rested on and by an order to go out and sacrifice that assumes a neglected duty.
It is simply a circumstance the lawgiver did not mention.
The exhortation to hope had been given and a witness of the deliverance stood among them, so the silence removes no excuse.

outliers.claim: Explains the lifted hand as the ancient gesture of an oath, a right hand raised to heaven, which lights up the psalm about a right hand of falsehood and survives in the courts of his own country.
Insists the narrative is plain history and not vision, and contrasts the single channel appointed for this people with the many the nations used, soothsayers, augurs and astrologers alike.

themes: And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, the tenth day of the month, that certain of the elders of Israel came to enquire of the Lord, and sat before me.
Then came the word of the Lord unto me, saying,
Son of man, speak unto the elders of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Are ye come to enquire of me? As I live, saith the Lord God, I will not be enquired of by you.
Wilt thou judge them, son of man, wilt thou judge them? cause them to know the abominations of their fathers:

And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; In the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up mine hand unto the seed of the house of Jacob, and made myself known unto them in the land of Egypt, when I lifted up mine hand unto them, saying, I am the Lord your God;
In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands:
Then said I unto them, Cast ye away every man the abominations of his eyes, and defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.

But they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me: they did not every man cast away the abominations of their eyes, neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt: then I said, I will pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

But I wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, among whom they were, in whose sight I made myself known unto them, in bringing them forth out of the land of Egypt.

10.pericope_label: Wherefore I caused them to go forth out of the land of Egypt, and brought them into the wilderness. And I gave them my statutes, and shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them. Moreover also I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord that sanctify them. But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness: they walked not in my statutes, and they despised my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; and my sabbaths they greatly polluted: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness, to consume them. But I wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, in whose sight I brought them out. Yet also I lifted up my hand unto them in the wilderness, that I would not bring them into the land which I had given them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands; Because they despised my judgments, and walked not in my statutes, but polluted my sabbaths: for their heart went after their idols. Nevertheless mine eye spared them from destroying them, neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks a second period here and lists what it held, the departure, the law, the tabernacle, the priesthood and the march to the border, guards against reading the demand as a perfunctory keeping of precepts rather than obedience from the heart while allowing the older covenant rightly called one of works, points out that the sabbath like circumcision was older than this period and here re-commanded as the covenant's special pledge, and specifies the sentence in the desert as falling on everyone over twenty at the departure while insisting mercy was not wholly withdrawn.

Gill dwells on a place where the people were wholly dependent and kept alive daily by miracle and notes it was the whole house for forty years, lists what the nations would have said had they died there, and gives the arithmetic of a generation dying but for two men; Calvin presses the motive that the cause of the deliverance was the divine glory, adds that ruling them familiarly by doctrine was a further generosity beyond the rescue, holds that the sons proved like their fathers with no excuse left after the law was published, draws their character from the failed threat since men who grow worse under punishment are desperate, reconciles the two accounts of the cause, and insists the restraint was no indulgence feeding their corruption.

Clarke undercuts their credit by noting they had to be forced out of a bondage they were unwilling to leave, says the law showed men what to do to be safe and wise so that heeding it would have made them holy, healthy and happy, calls the sabbath the first statute given to men and a token of creation, rest and inheritance together, observes that they behaved in the desert as in Egypt, and puts the sentence as disinheritance rather than destruction; Wesley says preserving life against beasts and barrenness was a continued miracle, states the exchange of fathers for children in a line, and reduces the sabbath to a badge of belonging.
Henry frames the passage as a struggle between sins working to ruin a nation and mercies working to save it, and notes that the wilderness story is held up later as a warning to Christian readers.

debates.question: Why is the sabbath singled out from the rest of the law?

positions.position: One precept is singled out to make the whole plainer, though set beside the commandments on strange gods and images the fourth looks lightest.
It was the first statute given to men and a token of three things at once, the creation behind, the rest ahead and the inheritance beyond.
It was older than this period, like circumcision, and here re-commanded as the covenant's special pledge.
A badge of belonging.

outliers.claim: Notes that the people had to be forced out of Egypt, being unwilling to leave a bondage that was oppressive and degrading.
Draws their character from the failure of the threat, since fools are corrected by punishment and men who grow worse under it show themselves desperate.

themes: Wherefore I caused them to go forth out of the land of Egypt, and brought them into the wilderness.
And I gave them my statutes, and shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them.
Moreover also I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord that sanctify them.

But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness: they walked not in my statutes, and they despised my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; and my sabbaths they greatly polluted: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness, to consume them.
But I wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, in whose sight I brought them out.
Yet also I lifted up my hand unto them in the wilderness, that I would not bring them into the land which I had given them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands;
Because they despised my judgments, and walked not in my statutes, but polluted my sabbaths: for their heart went after their idols.
Nevertheless mine eye spared them from destroying them, neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness.

18.pericope_label: But I said unto their children in the wilderness, Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers, neither observe their judgments, nor defile yourselves with their idols: I am the Lord your God; walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them; And hallow my sabbaths; and they shall be a sign between me and you, that ye may know that I am the Lord your God. Notwithstanding the children rebelled against me: they walked not in my statutes, neither kept my judgments to do them, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; they polluted my sabbaths: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the wilderness. Nevertheless I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted in the sight of the heathen, in whose sight I brought them forth. I lifted up mine hand unto them also in the wilderness, that I would scatter them among the heathen, and disperse them through the countries; Because they had not executed my judgments, but had despised my statutes, and had polluted my sabbaths, and their eyes were after their fathers’ idols. Wherefore I gave them also statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live; And I polluted them in their own gifts, in that they caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb, that I might make them desolate, to the end that they might know that I am the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott opens a third section on the generation grown up in the free air of the desert while warning that national characteristics rather than one generation are being described, denies that the oath of scattering was meant for that generation since the threat is given repeatedly to the nation as a whole and executed only when obstinacy made it unavoidable, argues that the statutes not good cannot be the ordinances a man lives by and so are no part of the law whatever many fathers supposed, rejects the escape that what was given was good in itself and only turned bad in the using, notes that the word for fire is supplied from a later verse, and identifies the custom as consecration to Moloch.

Gill takes the address for the exhortations delivered on the plains before the crossing, dates the sons' fall to the worship joined there, glosses hallowing as abstaining from business and attending religious duty, rejects the moral law as holy and just, notes that a law may be good to the keeper and deadly to the breaker, and inclines to ceremonial rites not good in their own nature; Calvin hears the change of audience as a verdict on fathers passed over as deaf, reads the declaration of who God is as claiming what men usurp when they set up as his partners and infect his law with commentary, insists that bare rest was never the sabbath's point, observes that command and promise both failed, makes the bad statutes a judicial handing over to another yoke, and explains that the people would have objected they had not abandoned the worship of God since they mixed the ceremonies with heathen inventions.

Clarke says the children were chosen in their fathers' stead, pictures the hand raised to crush and drawn back, loses patience with the noise the hard verse has made among believers and unbelievers alike and denies that God ever gave any people such statutes in the sense the words seem to bear, and insists the practice named was one God everywhere denounced; Wesley makes the withdrawing the posture of one about to strike who draws back to spare, states the bad statutes as not enjoined but permitted and pernicious to their users, and closes on the purpose that men who would not have him a gracious king in governing should own him a mighty one in punishing.

debates.question: What are the statutes that were not good?

positions.position: Not what the words seem to say at all: God never gave any people such statutes, and the sense is that they were left to their own way.
No part of the law, since they cannot be the ordinances a man lives by; nor will it do to say what was given was good in itself and turned bad in the using.
Not the moral law, which is holy and just, but ceremonial rites not good in their own nature.
A judicial handing over: men who refused to be governed by the law's doctrine were left to bear another yoke.

outliers.claim: Hears in the turn from fathers to sons a verdict on the fathers, who were passed over as deaf and past hope of repentance.
States the hard verse as a permission rather than a command, statutes not enjoined but allowed to be made and pernicious to those who used them.

themes: But I said unto their children in the wilderness, Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers, neither observe their judgments, nor defile yourselves with their idols:
I am the Lord your God; walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them;
And hallow my sabbaths; and they shall be a sign between me and you, that ye may know that I am the Lord your God.

Notwithstanding the children rebelled against me: they walked not in my statutes, neither kept my judgments to do them, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; they polluted my sabbaths: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the wilderness.
Nevertheless I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name’s sake, that it should not be polluted in the sight of the heathen, in whose sight I brought them forth.
I lifted up mine hand unto them also in the wilderness, that I would scatter them among the heathen, and disperse them through the countries;
Because they had not executed my judgments, but had despised my statutes, and had polluted my sabbaths, and their eyes were after their fathers’ idols.
Wherefore I gave them also statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live;
And I polluted them in their own gifts, in that they caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb, that I might make them desolate, to the end that they might know that I am the Lord.

27.pericope_label: Therefore, son of man, speak unto the house of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Yet in this your fathers have blasphemed me, in that they have committed a trespass against me. For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices, and there they presented the provocation of their offering: there also they made their sweet savour, and poured out there their drink offerings. Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day. Wherefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord God; Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers? and commit ye whoredom after their abominations? For when ye offer your gifts, when ye make your sons to pass through the fire, ye pollute yourselves with all your idols, even unto this day: and shall I be enquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, saith the Lord God, I will not be enquired of by you. And that which cometh into your mind shall not be at all, that ye say, We will be as the heathen, as the families of the countries, to serve wood and stone.

schools.summary: Ellicott opens the fourth period and remarks that the longest stretch of history gets the briefest treatment, charged with one offence, altars on every height, explains the name of the high place as simply meaning height while dismissing as fanciful the derivation that would make it a pun on the question, marks the fifth and last section as aimed at the prophet's contemporaries with questions that answer themselves, traces the ambition to be like the nations back to the original demand for a king, and notes that the Hebrew ends the chapter at the close of the promise so that the last five verses belong with what comes after.

Gill sets the ingratitude against what the entry had cost and says what was contrived will come to nothing; Calvin says the insult was intolerable because it came after possession was granted, explains that one altar in one place was the rule and even that unshaped before the nation had a fixed station so that high ground and thick shade were a standing invitation, admits the question about the high place looks flat and thinks commentators have missed that its point is the removal of any plea of ignorance, defends the interrogative against two older renderings, finds it barely credible that a people chastised out of their appetites should present themselves as willing to obey, and reads the delegation's real wish as despair reaching for a solution.

Clarke asks what a high place is good for and takes its name for a mark of infamy the people went on using, uses the verse about polluting themselves to settle the earlier crux since the polluting was self-inflicted and merely permitted, and answers the scheme of assimilation flatly, that the people will be kept distinct whether they wish it or not and the nations they court will despise them; Wesley makes the question a puzzle about attraction and spells out the programme as intermarriage, trade and religion together, taken for safety.
Henry sharpens the aggravation, since the fathers had watched where the same conduct led and repeated it, and warning wasted is worse than warning never given.

debates.question: What did the elders who came to enquire actually want?

positions.position: Despair reaching for a solution: hated for worshipping a God of their own, they judged nothing would serve better than to give up entirely and take the manners of the nations.
A long-standing ambition to be like the nations round about, shown already in the original demand for a king and a chief cause of the idolatrous tendency.
Naturalisation among idolaters, which cannot succeed since they will be kept distinct and despised by those they court.
Union with them in marriage, commerce and religion, undertaken for safety.

outliers.claim: Explains that even the first altar was to be unshaped, a mound of turf or rough stone, so that a landscape of high ground and thick shade was a standing invitation to build elsewhere.
Notes that the Hebrew and the ancient versions end the chapter at the close of the promise, so that the last five verses belong with the following chapter.

themes: Therefore, son of man, speak unto the house of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Yet in this your fathers have blasphemed me, in that they have committed a trespass against me.

For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices, and there they presented the provocation of their offering: there also they made their sweet savour, and poured out there their drink offerings.
Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day.
Wherefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord God; Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers? and commit ye whoredom after their abominations?

For when ye offer your gifts, when ye make your sons to pass through the fire, ye pollute yourselves with all your idols, even unto this day: and shall I be enquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, saith the Lord God, I will not be enquired of by you.
And that which cometh into your mind shall not be at all, that ye say, We will be as the heathen, as the families of the countries, to serve wood and stone.

33.pericope_label: As I live, saith the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you: And I will bring you out from the people, and will gather you out of the countries wherein ye are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face. Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so will I plead with you, saith the Lord God. And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant: And I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me: I will bring them forth out of the country where they sojourn, and they shall not enter into the land of Israel: and ye shall know that I am the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott shows the reply built out of the exodus, the formula of a mighty hand and stretched-out arm being the standing phrase of the law for the acts that brought the people out but joined here to fury poured out on themselves, argues that the gathering cannot mean restoration since it is an act of wrath whose destination is a desert, declines to locate the wilderness at all since the phrase about pleading face to face is meant by sense and not letter, makes the counting under the rod an examination that reconstitutes a covenant people, and observes how the sifting worked itself out through ordinary causes at the actual return.

Gill notes the oath by the divine life, names the refuges among which the fugitives meant to settle, offers three possibilities for the wilderness and inclines to the long dispersion, turns the rod toward correction that brings men to confession, and treats rebel and transgressor as one charge stated twice; Calvin explains that dispersion had felt like release from jurisdiction so that men who thought themselves disinherited thought themselves free, sets the whole stage between rejection and reconciliation since release from Chaldea might have been mistaken for simple favour, insists the word is a shepherd's crook and not a sceptre or a stick for beating, takes the counting as proof of ownership, and resists reading the purging as favour since the verb means to pick out and drag the hidden into light.

Clarke takes the wilderness of the land itself, found desolate on return, and says the dealing there will either end them or mend them, gives the rabbinic detail of the tithing of sheep in full, the flock penned and a rod dipped in vermilion marking the tenth as it passed, and extends the sentence to his own day; Wesley names the remote mountainous regions and calls them the most horrid parts of the world, makes the muster one in which men either own the sceptre or are subdued by force, and reduces the rebels to the stubborn.
Henry states what is being frustrated, a plan to dissolve into the nations which will fail because the compliant will not be allowed to share their neighbours' prosperity.

debates.question: What is the wilderness of the peoples?

positions.position: Babylon, or the inhospitable countries many were carried into, or the road home; most likely the long dispersion the nation was still living in.
The remote mountainous regions north and east, the most horrid parts of the world.
The land itself, found desolate on the return, where the dealing will either end them or mend them.
Not locatable: as the past had its probation in a desert so will the future, and the phrase is meant by sense rather than letter.

outliers.claim: Gives the rabbinic account of tithing sheep in full, the flock penned at a gap wide enough for one and a rod dipped in vermilion marking the tenth as it passed.
Observes that the promised sifting worked itself out through ordinary causes at the actual return, two prosperous generations abroad against a homeland lying waste and ringed with enemies.

themes: As I live, saith the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you:
And I will bring you out from the people, and will gather you out of the countries wherein ye are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out.
And I will bring you into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face.
Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so will I plead with you, saith the Lord God.
And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant:

And I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me: I will bring them forth out of the country where they sojourn, and they shall not enter into the land of Israel: and ye shall know that I am the Lord.

39.pericope_label: As for you, O house of Israel, thus saith the Lord God; Go ye, serve ye every one his idols, and hereafter also, if ye will not hearken unto me: but pollute ye my holy name no more with your gifts, and with your idols. For in mine holy mountain, in the mountain of the height of Israel, saith the Lord God, there shall all the house of Israel, all of them in the land, serve me: there will I accept them, and there will I require your offerings, and the firstfruits of your oblations, with all your holy things. I will accept you with your sweet savour, when I bring you out from the people, and gather you out of the countries wherein ye have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you before the heathen. And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall bring you into the land of Israel, into the country for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to your fathers. And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed. And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I have wrought with you for my name’s sake, not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the permission to serve idols the most fearful punishment imaginable, being allowed to follow one's chosen road to the end, holds the middle ground on the holy mountain by allowing that nothing there need mean more than the return from exile while thinking the parallel with an earlier and plainly Messianic passage makes a longer view hard to avoid, warns against forcing any single phrase into direct fulfilment, and takes the narrower historical view that idolatry was cured once for all at the restoration and never nationally resumed, noting that the prophecy and the Hebrew chapter both end here.

Gill takes the mountain of the church for firmness, holiness and visibility, turns the sweet savour to expiation and imputed righteousness, lists what is learned by experience and afterwards publicly owned, and extends the shame to a rejection he sees continuing; Calvin locates the offence in mixture rather than open apostasy since the people supposed a half worship acceptable while still owning the true God, says the address has turned to the elect in whom the church was to survive, explains that the language of sweet savour is the legal formula and does not mean incense was agreeable in itself, distinguishes the knowledge that tastes a father's love from the knowledge the condemned have of a judge, insists there is no reconciliation without repentance intervening, and gives the last word to a glory shown in pity spent on the abandoned for the sake of a name.

Clarke uses the permission to close the earlier crux about statutes not good, takes the mountain of a day when the true sacrifice is received and thanks brought in for a gift beyond speech, reduces the promised knowledge to an acknowledgment, and allows the promise a limited application to the return from Babylon while placing its proper fulfilment later; Wesley keeps the mountain literal, a hill lower than many but raised above them by a presence, with temple rebuilt and offerings required as before, says that while men are idolaters they should keep the name out of their mouths, and takes the sanctifying as the praise God earns by the good he does his people.

debates.question: How far does the promise of the holy mountain reach?

positions.position: To the literal restoration, temple rebuilt, city repeopled and offerings required as before.
To the church, gathered where the true sacrifice is received.
Nothing here need mean more than the return from exile, though the parallel with an earlier Messianic passage makes a longer view hard to avoid; no single phrase should be forced.
To the elect remnant in whom the church was to survive.

outliers.claim: Holds that idolatry, the sin of all the earlier ages, was cured once for all at the restoration and never nationally resumed, whatever else was done afterwards.
Warns that men, the devout included, take an offered pardon greedily and bury their sins under it, so that no reconciliation comes without repentance intervening.

themes: As for you, O house of Israel, thus saith the Lord God; Go ye, serve ye every one his idols, and hereafter also, if ye will not hearken unto me: but pollute ye my holy name no more with your gifts, and with your idols.

For in mine holy mountain, in the mountain of the height of Israel, saith the Lord God, there shall all the house of Israel, all of them in the land, serve me: there will I accept them, and there will I require your offerings, and the firstfruits of your oblations, with all your holy things.
I will accept you with your sweet savour, when I bring you out from the people, and gather you out of the countries wherein ye have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you before the heathen.
And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall bring you into the land of Israel, into the country for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to your fathers.
And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed.

And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I have wrought with you for my name’s sake, not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel, saith the Lord God.

45.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, set thy face toward the south, and drop thy word toward the south, and prophesy against the forest of the south field; And say to the forest of the south, Hear the word of the Lord; Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein. And all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it: it shall not be quenched. Then said I, Ah Lord God! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the first of the three words for south as that which lies on the right hand; Ellicott shows that one English word stands for three different Hebrew ones, the right hand since a speaker faces east, the bright or noonday quarter, and the dry country, answers the objection that the target lay nearly west by pointing out that an army from Babylon could only reach it from the north because of the intervening desert, takes the green and dry trees of moral condition and presses that a national judgment sweeps away all together with no allowance for those less ripe in evil, notes that the prophet drops the figure for the thing meant when he reaches the phrase about faces, and takes the obscurity as deliberate, a device to sharpen attention for the coming explanation.

Gill notes that a fresh oracle begins here and that several editors start a new chapter at this verse, takes the set face for speaking boldly and as a token that God had set his face against the place, agrees that neighbours as well as sufferers will see whose hand it is, and offers three senses for the closing protest, a plea not to be sent, a plea not to be sent in figures, or a plea against the calamity, recording a Greek rendering that makes it a flat refusal.

Clarke identifies the forest with the city, as thick with people as a wood with trees, reads the fire as war with the green tree for the substantial citizens and the dry for the meanest, runs the terror the length of a country lying north and south, and turns the protest into an anticipation of the audience, who put the evil day far off and dismiss the speaker as a maker of riddles whose meaning need not be reached and may not concern their own time; Wesley notes that the verb for prophesying is to distil, so that softer speech comes first and the storm afterwards, matches Clarke on the trees, and reports the complaint that the speaker cannot be understood at all.
Henry says these lines have no connection with what precedes and are expounded by what follows, so that the chapter is broken in the wrong place.

debates.question: Why is the message put in a parable the hearers reject as unintelligible?

positions.position: Deliberately, as elsewhere in this prophet, to sharpen attention for the explanation about to be given.
The obscurity becomes their excuse: they put the evil day far off and dismiss the speaker as a maker of riddles whose meaning need not be reached.
The protest may be against being sent at all, against being sent in figures, or against the calamity itself.

outliers.claim: Explains why a country lying nearly west of the speaker is called the south, since an army from Babylon could only approach it from the north on account of the intervening desert.
Notes that the verb for prophesying here means to distil, so that the message begins with softer words before it comes down as a storm.

themes: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,
Son of man, set thy face toward the south, and drop thy word toward the south, and prophesy against the forest of the south field;

And say to the forest of the south, Hear the word of the Lord; Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein.
And all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it: it shall not be quenched.
Then said I, Ah Lord God! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?
